articles.excerpt: Global music industry revenues are expected to reach approximately $200 billion annually by 2035 amid an improving outlook for subscription streaming. New subscription models, AI, and direct-to-consumer offerings are creating opportunities for the industry to reach audiences in new ways, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The music market undershot growth expectations over the last several years. The new forecast represents the first time in three years that Goldman Sachs Research has raised its long-term outlook for the industry, Stephen Laszczyk and Eric Sheridan write in the team’s 2026 edition of the annual “Music in the Air” report. Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to increase at 6.7% year-on-year in 2026 and at a compound rate of 5.8% per year between 2025 and 2035. “While growth is likely to moderate from the pace observed during the industry's streaming adoption phase, we continue to see a long runway for industry expansion supported by favorable consumer behavior and an increasingly diversified monetization model,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write. Paid streaming subscriptions are helping to shore up the outlook for recorded music. After three consecutive downgrades to its forecast for 2030 recorded music revenues, Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for the segment this year reflects improvements in streaming revenue, physical revenue, and download and other digital revenue. Subscription streaming revenue is growing faster, mainly because subscriber numbers are increasing more quickly than expected and revenue per user is rising in developed markets. articles.title: Emerging Market Credit Shows Resilience amid Energy Shock
articles.excerpt: When the Iran war triggered a surge in oil prices this year, many investors may have expected credit markets in the developing world to slide into a selloff. Instead, emerging market sovereign and corporate bonds weathered the shock with a newfound stability and solid performance for investors. The development is a key sign that emerging market credit is maturing into a resilient asset class, according to Anupam Damani, co-head and senior portfolio manager of emerging market debt at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. At the same time, investors are rethinking their approach to the market, which has trillions of dollars in outstanding debt. “Emerging market credit is now unrecognizable, and I mean that in a good way,” Damani says. “These bonds used to come with a crisis label, but this market is no longer monolithic. In my view, it has become a more diverse and resilient asset class, though risks remain.” To be sure, emerging market bonds run the gamut in terms of risk, and investors must be selective about what they trade in a marketplace with myriad issuers, she adds.

articles.title: The Rise of Healthcare Consumerism | Morgan Stanley
articles.excerpt: U.S. consumers are increasingly taking the lead in how they access and pay for healthcare, creating potential opportunities across biopharma and healthcare services. In the complex and costly U.S. healthcare system, patients are no longer just heeding drug ads to “Ask Your Doctor”—they’re going straight to the source. Policy changes and technological advances have given consumers more ways to directly choose the healthcare products and services that best suit their needs—including care, testing and medicines—as well as how they pay for them. The healthcare industry is adapting to this trend, potentially creating new opportunities for investors. In biopharma alone, the total direct-to-consumer cash-pay market could reach $26 billion at its peak. Eyeing that opportunity, many large-cap biopharma companies now offer direct-to-consumer platforms. Healthcare consumerism took root with the creation of Health Savings Accounts (HSAs) in 2003, followed by the growth of high-deductible health plans (HDHPs). These changes gave consumers more control over healthcare spending—but also shifted more of the costs and decisions to them.

articles.link_title: How AI Agents Could Disrupt Consumer Industries
articles.title: Winners and Losers From AI Agents | Morgan Stanley
articles.excerpt: As AI agents become more capable of making decisions and purchases on consumers’ behalf, Morgan Stanley Research examines which industries could benefit—and which face growing competitive pressure. The recent launch of powerful consumer AI agents has reignited debate over how artificial intelligence could disrupt industries ranging from retail and insurance to transportation and live entertainment. Unlike traditional AI tools that primarily answer questions, these agents can browse websites, complete forms, compare prices, make purchases and even help negotiate bills. Morgan Stanley Research estimates that roughly $30 trillion in consumer spending could be digitized through AI agents across online advertising, e-commerce, travel, food delivery, ridesharing, logistics, wearables and other sectors. The extent of the disruption will depend on how quickly consumers adopt AI agents and how effectively companies make money from agent-driven activity and transactions.

articles.excerpt: The AI buildout is accelerating, bringing binding constraints forward. We stay overweight U.S. equities and upgrade emerging market stocks to overweight but stay focused on opportunities driven by bottlenecks. Global government bond yields have surged through the summer. Higher yields have restored income opportunities, but only via a flexible approach. We prefer short-term bonds over long-term bonds with high sensitivity to interest rates. Asset-class buckets are a less useful starting point in a world shaped by mega forces. Infrastructure shows why: Its exposure to AI demand, energy security and fragmentation runs across markets and asset classes. The AI investment boom is having two broad impacts: lifting activity and earnings while absorbing more capital, power, materials and balance-sheet capacity. Heavy sovereign borrowing is adding to the demand for funding. The result is a higher cost of capital even as AI boosts growth. These developments reinforce our core Midyear Outlook themes: AI has the potential to deliver a sustained increase in growth and productivity, but that path to abundances runs through scarcity in capital, materials and labor.

articles.excerpt: Higher yields have changed the fixed income opportunity. More of a portfolio's potential return can come from income, even as persistent inflation tests bonds' traditional diversification role and diverging economic cycles create different investment conditions across markets. The challenge is no longer simply finding yield, but understanding which risks investors are being paid to take. Income may be abundant, but it is not interchangeable; similar yields can carry very different risks. With policy rates and longer-term yields moving higher, investors are weighing how much risk higher rates pose to different parts of the economy. Growth remains resilient overall, but rate sensitivity varies significantly across sectors and households, while some inflation pressures are less responsive to rates. Today’s starting yields may allow investors to generate attractive income without reaching as far for it. Investors are questioning what is keeping long-term yields elevated and what that means for bonds in portfolios. Inflation is only part of the answer: stronger nominal growth, greater competition for capital and diminished diversification benefits are also contributing to higher yields. That combination strengthens fixed income’s role as a source of income, even as persistent inflation makes its diversification benefits more conditional. Higher European bond yields have improved the income opportunity, but tighter spreads leave less room for broad spread compression to drive returns. articles.title: Beyond CCCs, high-yield appears resilient
articles.excerpt: Is the high-yield bond market sending a warning? Spreads on CCC-rated bonds have widened by more than 500 basis points from their lowest levels this year, to roughly 1,000 basis points over Treasuries. Meanwhile, spreads on higher-quality BB- and B-rated bonds have remained relatively contained. Because of their lower credit quality, CCC-rated bonds typically trade at a discount to the rest of high-yield. That discount is now larger than at any point since the COVID-19 market sell-off, raising investor concern about broader credit deterioration. The important question is whether the cracks at the bottom of the high-yield market are a signal for the broader credit market. A closer look at the Bloomberg U.S. Corporate High Yield Index suggests the picture is more nuanced: stress is concentrated, the market is higher quality than in the past, and attractive income opportunities remain. Four out of more than 150 CCC-rated issuers make up more than 30% of current CCC-rated bond spreads. Many of the companies most affected are in the telecommunications and media sector, where secular headwinds and company-specific challenges are driving distress. In other words, this has not been an indiscriminate repricing of credit risk. But that doesn’t mean investors should ignore it. Financial conditions have tightened this year. Interest rates on the broad U.S. bond market have increased by nearly 100 basis points, and this tightening is filtering through to parts of the credit market. Distress often appears first in the lowest-quality companies, which is not uncommon in the later stages of the credit cycle.

The IRS requires that most owners of IRAs withdraw part of their tax-deferred savings each year, starting at age 731 or after inheriting any IRA account for certain individual beneficiaries.2 That withdrawal is known as a required minimum distribution (RMD). RMDs are designed to ensure that investments in IRAs don't grow tax-deferred forever, and this carries over to the beneficiary of the IRA. The rules for how IRA beneficiaries must take RMDs will depend on when the original account owner passed away. The Setting Every Community Up for Retirement Enhancement (SECURE) Act of 2019, followed by SECURE 2.0 in 2022, brought changes to the rules for inherited IRAs—most notably, by changing the "stretch IRA" strategy for most nonspouse beneficiaries. This allowed nonspouse beneficiaries to "stretch" RMDs over their own life expectancy; by introducing the 10‑year rule, most nonspouse beneficiaries are now required to fully withdraw the inherited IRA balance by the end of the 10th year following the original account owner's death. These changes affect beneficiaries of account owners who passed away on or after January 1, 2020. Beneficiaries of account owners who passed away before 2020 may continue to use the lifetime distribution rules.

Make the most of your savings by understanding the key differences between Roth and traditional IRAs: There are two types of IRAs, and choosing between a Roth IRA and a traditional IRA often depends on your current financial situation and your anticipated tax bracket in retirement. Roth IRAs offer tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, making them an attractive option for those who expect to be in a higher tax bracket in the future. Traditional IRAs provide tax-deferred growth with pre-tax contributions, which can be helpful for those seeking a tax break in the current tax year. Eligibility requirements for traditional and Roth IRAs differ primarily based on income levels and tax filing status. Traditional IRAs generally allow anyone with earned income to contribute, but tax deductibility is phased out at higher income levels if the contributor or their spouse has access to a workplace retirement plan. In contrast, Roth IRAs have income caps beyond which individuals cannot contribute at all. Determining eligibility is important before choosing which IRA to open because it ensures that contributors select the type that maximizes their tax advantages and aligns with their financial situation and retirement goals. articles.excerpt: Learn what an emergency fund is, review the simple steps to build a fund that’s tailored to your needs, and explore additional resources to help maximize your savings. An emergency fund is an amount of money set aside in a dedicated savings account to help provide a financial safety net for life’s unexpected challenges. Common emergencies like unexpected medical bills, car troubles, or job loss can be overwhelming—but with an emergency fund, you can face these challenges with peace of mind. When is $2,000 as powerful as $1,000,000? Our research shows, $2,000 in an emergency fund can be just as powerful as having $1M in assets when it comes to your financial well-being. Think about it: If you’re lost in the desert and fighting heat and thirst, it only takes a small amount of water to keep you going. You could have all the water in the world back home, but you would get immediate relief from a much smaller amount that’s available right then and there. Your emergency fund is like water in the desert. Just $2,000 can give you a buffer against many of the things life can throw at you. Spending shocks are unplanned expenses like a broken windshield or a root canal. Saving enough to cover at least half a month’s worth of living expenses can help you prepare for potential spending shocks. Income shocks are the unplanned loss of income. While these events may happen less frequently, they can be a significant setback to your financial plan. Over time, you should aim to build three to six months' worth of living expenses in your emergency fund to prepare for potential income shocks.
